R. v. Mahr
, 2010 ONCJ 216

ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE

HER
MAJESTY THE QUEEN

v.

MAX
MAHR

CHARGES:
s. 319(2) C.C.C. – Incite Hatred

R
E A S O N S   F O R   S E N T E N C E

by
the Honourable Justice N. S. Douglas

on

Counsel for the Crown

Counsel for Max Mahr

MONDAY, MAY 10, 2010
.

R E A S O N S   F O R   S E N
T E N C E

N. S. DOUGLAS, J. (Orally):

Max Mahr pled
guilty before me to count one of a multi-count information that says between
the 2nd day of January 2009 and the 29th day of September 2009, at the City of
Guelph, he did by communicating statements; “God Help Kill All Jews, Kill All
Jews, God Help Exterminate Jews, God Help No Israel, Exterminate Israel,
Exterminate All Evil Jews, Do Good Kill Jews, Kill Evil Jews” wilfully promote
hatred against an identifiable group to wit: the Jewish people, contrary to the

Criminal Code of Canada
, section 319(2).

The Crown
Attorney received the consent of the Attorney General in order to proceed with
this charge and proceeded by indictment.

The defence
pled guilty before this court.  Section 319(2) says that:

Every one who,
by communicating statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully
promotes hatred against any identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an
indictable offence and is likely to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two
years...

His plea was
under
section 319(2)
, the wilful promotion of hatred.

Section
718.2(a)(i) reads as follows:

A court that
imposes a sentence shall also take into consideration the following
principles:  (a) sentence should be increased or reduced to account for any
relevant aggravating or mitigating circumstances relating to the offence or the
offender, and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing,(i) evidence
that the offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on race, national
or ethnic origin, language, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or physical
disability, sexual orientation, or any other similar factor, shall be deemed to
be aggravating circumstances.

This crime is
motivated in my view, by hate based on race, national or ethnic origin, and
therefore, is a crime that shall be deemed to have the aggravating circumstance
as described in section 718.2.

The
communication here that wilfully promoted hatred against an identifiable group
is very obvious.  By an agreed statement of fact, the accused on 19 separate
occasions, from the time span alleged in the information, namely over an
approximate eight to nine month period, attended at various places in the
community of Guelph, public places; parks, many washrooms in the Stone Road
Mall, Wal-Mart and different businesses, to write on the walls the messages
that are contained in count one, obviously promoting genocide, urging other
people to kill all members of the Jewish race.

While there
are cases that assist me in my responsibility today and I am going to cite a
few of them; there are no other cases that I am aware of, or that counsel has
advised me of, where the accused is a man who grew up in Germany, prior to
World War II, fought in World War II, and at the time of these offences in
2009, embraced the same mindset that led to the Holocaust.

In the case of
R. v.
Keegstra
, the
Supreme Court

of Canada
said back in
1989, that:

Parliament has
recognized the substantial harm that can flow from hate propaganda and in trying
to prevent the pain suffered by target group members, and to reduce racial
ethnic and religious tension and perhaps even violence in Canada; has decided
to suppress the wilful promotion of hatred against identifiable groups.
Parliament’s objective is supported not only by the work of numerous study
groups, but also by our collective historical knowledge of the potentially
catastrophic effects of the promotion of hatred.

Section 319(2)
then, when breached requires the court to send out a strong message of
condemnation both reinforcing the values underlying section 319(2) and
deterring the few individuals who would harm target group members and the
larger community by communicating hate propaganda, will occasionally require
the use of the criminal law.

In a case
called R. v.
Lelas
, [1990] 58 C.C.C. 3rd, p. 568; the Ontario Court of
Appeal
,
had an opportunity to review a sentence where the accused,

Lelas
was sentenced to six months imprisonment and two years probation.
The Crown appealed that sentence imposed by a justice of the Ontario Court of
Justice.  The crime involved spray painting synagogues with swastikas and a
message, smash the ZOG; ZOG being an acronym for Zionist Occupational
Government.  They left a sign on the synagogue and came upon a Hebrew school
and spray painted Nazism and a swastika on the school sign, and some other
messages.

The accused,
at the time of his arrest was found to be in possession of three Nazi flags, a
framed photograph of Adolf Hitler, and a framed membership in the Ku Klux Klan,
and a Ku Klux Klan robe.  He was born in 1967, describing himself as a national
socialist.

A member of
the Canadian Jewish Congress testified in that case and in describing the
impact of the spray painting said this:

One can
understand then that anyone approaching a synagogue, anyone seeing this in the
media, would have an immediate emotional type of reaction.  Some people that I
spoke to directly indicated that it’s this type of thing that they feared the
most after the Holocaust and coming to Canada, was the manifestations of
anti-Semitism and manifestations of Neo-Nazis and the fear of its
reoccurrence.  Even if it may not be correct, that fear was so present and so
much a part of their concern that we couldn’t help but fear it again, not only
in terms of Toronto, but certainly from various communities across the country.

The reaction
of this type of crime according to the member of the Canadian Jewish Congress,
varied from absolute fear to outrage.

The court said
at paragraph 30 in the
Court of Appeal
:

In spray
painting a synagogue and Hebrew School,
Lelas
was not merely intending
to cause damage to property, rather to use his words, he wanted to enrage the
Jewish community.  His acts were done to strike fear and terror, and to cause
emotional upset in the Jewish community.  When mischief is racially or
religiously motivated and is done to cause emotional injury or shock to a
particular segment of Canadian society, it calls for a far more severe penalty
than mischief, which is done merely to damage property.  A sentence of six
months is not, in my opinion, sufficient to meet the needs of general
deterrence and to show society’s abhorrence of the acts of the respondent.  If
it were not for the fact that
Lelas
has been released and must be
re-incarcerated, I would have imposed a longer sentence.  The message must go
out loud and clear that conduct such as that engaged in by the respondent, will
not be tolerated in Canadian society and if it is engaged in, it will be met
with a severe penalty.  Accordingly, I would allow the appeal and increase the
sentence to one year concurrent on each count.

In the present
case of Max Mahr, some might say this is an old man and World War II ended 65
years ago; why does this case have any significance to the communities today?

As I see this
case, the crime itself was not committed 65 years ago.  Mr. Mahr has brought
this poisonous hatred into the 21st century and he goes on a mission.  That’s
what it was, to wilfully promote, incite, encourage, the very same thing that
happened to the Jewish community so many years ago.  And this is what makes
this case today so troubling.  I am not sentencing a man for something he did
65 years ago.  Every Jewish person alive today can be said to be a victim of
his crime, clearly every Holocaust survivor.

But these are
not the only members of the public who have an interest in the result of this
case today.  And it is not just the veterans of World War II.  It is not just
the German Canadians; people who were all vilified and blamed for the acts of
the Nazi Regime, but in my view all Canadians today who value the basic
freedoms that we enjoy, have a direct interest in what happens today.

The accused
took advantage of those freedoms.  He was welcomed to Canada after the war and
he reaped all the benefits of the freedom that is so precious to all Canadians,
and he breached the trust that Canadians gave him by welcoming him here,
because it was that same heartless, merciless, cruel mindset of the Nazi Regime
that he brings with him.  And then by his actions, not just his thoughts, by
his actions over a period of several months he sneaks around in a cowardly way
and urges others to kill all Jews.  The ugly messages that he wrote evoke those
pictures that we have seen of Jewish children being led to the furnaces and the
gas chambers.  That is what those messages do.  That is what they do to all
Canadians.

There is a
victim impact statement filed here as well by a member of the Canadian Jewish
Congress, a man by the name of Len Rudner, who is the Regional Director of
Ontario for the Canadian Jewish Congress and I just want to refer to a few
things that he says.

Criminal
actions such as the uttering of threats, harassment and assault have the effect
of causing fear, anxiety and harm in the victim.

While the
content of many of these messages: God help kill all Jews; kill evil Jews;
exterminate Israel; do good kill Jews; Jew means evil – is odious, why are such
statements made in the public square (parks, malls, a Wal-Mart Store)?  Words,
for better or for worse, have the ability to transform people’s minds.  While
the connection between evil words and evil deeds may not be identified with
certainty, history is replete with examples of how language can prepare the ground
for the most tragic events.  As Alexander Tsesis notes in “
Destructive
Messages”
;

“Decades of
anti-Semitic literature had deluded common Germans into believing that the Jews
manipulated the world economy.  The ideology was so deeply entrenched that it
seemed logical to them to round up Jews, put them in concentration camps, and
eventually try to exterminate them.”

For our
community, the lessons of history are not easily forgotten.  Indeed the
memories of those brutal days are still alive in the minds of survivors, some
of whom live within a few kilometres of the hateful acts of anti-Semitism
engaged in by Mr. Mahr.

I have read
the pre-sentence report.  While Mr. Mahr now says that he has learned his
lesson and is sorry for what he has done, there is still a suggestion in the
pre-sentence report that he sees himself as a victim and justifies in some
measure what he did because he was discriminated against; he was vilified as a
German person who came to Canada and was treated badly.  I want to quote a few
things that he said from his interview with Constable Kevin King back in
September of 2009.

At page 9 of
the interview he says this.  Constable King says:

Q.  What are
your thoughts on the war back then and how that worked out?

The accused says:

A.  I believe
Hitler was right at the time.  I didn’t know any better.  I was teached like
that and now I know the difference.

Well if he
knows the difference, then why does he go out and do the same things that
Hitler did?  At page 14 of the interview he says first of all that he believes
Hitler was a Jew and he married a Jew.  He calls her Eva Braum, but it was Eva
Braun, B-R-A-U-N and not B-R-A-U-M.  He doesn’t even have her name right, but
he says:

Yeah and they
had a big hide out in the Alps, where is it, in Innsbruck; they call the Eagles
Nest and now they call it the Crow’s Nest.  I went there too, just to see.  Eva
Braum had a special room for her there.

So Constable
King says:  Q.  He’s Jewish?  His wife is Jewish?

Mahr says;
Yeah and Constable King says:  Q.  He did all these horrible things?  And Mahr
says:

A.  But you
don’t know if it’s true.  Maybe some of it is true.  It was not Hitler alone.
There was Hitler and there was all the others.  Some of them were Jews too.

And says Heishman
was a Jew.  I think he probably means Eichmann.

Q.  Who?

A.
Heishman.

Q.
Okay.

And Mahr
says:  A.  Typical Jew.

Think about
that for a moment, typical Jew.  Then he says:

After the war -
and Germany was no good anymore.  Everything was just for Jews.  No matter what
the Jews did, they were always right, always were the Jews.

And so while
he professes to be sorry and to now see the truth, that kind of language that
he uses during a free flowing interview displays and reveals that his remorse,
in my view, is remorse for being caught because he had to be caught.  That is
what he is sorry about in my view.

So what is the
proper sentence here?  Well, he has no record.  He has pled guilty.  He is 83
and his lawyer has worked hard for him and is urging the court not to send him
to traditional jail, but to grant him a conditional sentence, which the
community knows as house arrest.  And the Crown Attorney, who has also worked
hard on this case, has come to the conclusion that it is his view that a
conditional sentence would meet the ends of justice and he joins defence
counsel.  And so it is a joint submission put to me for a conditional
sentence.

What is my
responsibility when I am faced with a joint submission?  It is twofold.  Number
one, I should accept it, unless in my view, it does not satisfy the ends of
justice and is a sentence that in my interpretation of the law, as I apply it
to these facts, would bring the administration of justice into disrepute and
would offend the public conscience.  But that is not my only responsibility
with regard to a joint submission.  I must also put counsel on notice that I am
in a position where I believe the law requires me to sentence him to real jail,
and I must give counsel, particularly the Crown, an opportunity to explain why
he believes a joint submission is the proper sentence here and to try to show
me if I disagree with him, the error that I would make if I rejected the joint
submission.  In other words, I am not to blindside counsel.

I am going to
say now what I believe both counsel will agree with and I invite either one of
them to stand and interrupt me if they do not.  I pre-tried this matter.  This
matter was always on a guilty plea track and we discussed, both counsel and I,
in a general way what the options were with regard to sentence.  While I have
no notes of the pre-trial, I am confident that I expressed to both of them that
in my view, this would not be a proper case for a conditional sentence; that I
would remain open to hearing counsel’s submissions.  But I believe I made it
very clear to both of them that my initial impression of this case was that a
conditional sentence would not be a proper one.  That is the first thing I want
to say.

The second
thing I want to say is this; while counsel were making their submissions to me,
I made it clear to the Crown particularly, that I would need to be convinced
and my mind would have to be changed by the submissions of Crown counsel, and I
believe the Crown had an opportunity, knowing that I needed some persuading,
and that I might not be accepting the joint submission; to put his views
clearly on the record.

The third
thing I want to say is I don’t believe that either counsel will be genuinely
surprised if I reject the joint submission.  As a matter of fact, I believe
that both counsel know that that is a very real possibility today and no one is
going to be taken by surprise if I reject the joint submission.

Having given
both counsel an opportunity to rise, and neither one of them doing so, I am now
going to continue.  Why do I believe the law requires me to sentence Mr. Mahr
to real jail?  I think I can sum it up in one word; denunciation.  This may be
the last opportunity a Canadian Court has to look into the eyes of a member of the
German military during World War II and state clearly to him and to the public,
what all Canadians think of these acts of the accused, which came from the same
type of mind that led to the deaths of six million Jewish men, women and
children.  It would be a wrong message to grant Max Mahr a conditional
sentence.  It would be wrong morally and legally in my understanding of the
law.  Therefore, I would like you to stand up Mr. Mahr please.

I sentence you
to six months imprisonment to be followed by a period of two years probation
with the following terms:

Within one
business day of your release from custody, you will report to and be under the
supervision of a probation officer.  You will report as often as is required.

You will take
any counselling as required by the probation officer.

You are going
to perform 40 hours of community service at the discretion of the community
service coordinator and I will recommend that it be some community service
appropriate to the crime that you have committed, perhaps cleaning graffiti
after some of the hooliganism that happens in our town most Fridays and
Saturdays.

You will keep
the peace and you will be of good behaviour.

You will take
any counselling as required, as I have said, by the probation officer and sign
all appropriate release forms to confirm that.

I will waive
the victim fine surcharge.  That is the sentence of the court.  You take your
seat in custody now Mr. Mahr.  All right gentlemen, thank you.
